source_text: Potest uero et sic intellegi, ut qui saeculo renuntiauimus et diuitias eius et pompas fide gratiae spiritalis abiecimus cibum nobis tantum petamus et uictum, quando instruat Dominus et dicat: qui non renuntiat omnibus quae sunt eius, non potest meus discipulus esse. qui autem Christi coepit esse discipulus secundum magistri sui uocem renuntians omnibus, diurnum debet cibum petere nec in longum desideria petitionis extendere ipso iterum Domino praescribente et dicente: nolite in crastinum cogitare: crastinus enim dies ipse cogitabit sibi. sufficit diei malitia sua. merito ergo Christi discipulus uictum sibi in diem postulat qui de crastino cogitare prohibetur, quia et contrarium sibi fit et repugnans, ut quaeramus in saeculo diu uiuere qui petimus regnum Dei uelociter aduenire. sic et beatus apostolus monet formans et corroborans spei nostrae ac fidei firmitatem. nihil, inquit, intulimus in hunc mundum, uerum nec auferre possumus. habentes itaque exhibitionem et tegumentum his contenti sumus. qui autem uolunt diuites fieri incidunt in temptationem et muscipulas et desideria multa et nocentia quae mergunt hominem in perditionem et in interitum. radix enim omnium malorum est cupiditas quam quidam adpetentes naufragauerunt a fide et inseruerunt se doloribus multis.
thought_title: Daily bread as contentment, not long-term desire
orientation: Cyprian is explaining the petition for daily bread, now arguing that it teaches Christians to ask only for each day's food and not to plan far ahead.
pass_a_gloss: But it can also be understood thus: we who have renounced the world and have cast away its riches and its pomps by the faith of spiritual grace, let us ask for ourselves only food and sustenance, since the Lord instructs and says: he who does not renounce all things that are his cannot be my disciple. But he who has begun to be a disciple of Christ, renouncing all things according to the voice of his master, ought to ask for daily food and not to stretch out the desires of his petition into the long term, since the Lord himself again prescribes and says: do not think about tomorrow; for tomorrow's day will think about itself. Sufficient for the day is its own evil. Therefore rightly does the disciple of Christ ask for sustenance for himself for the day, who is forbidden to think about tomorrow, because it becomes contrary to himself and repugnant, that we should seek to live long in the world, we who ask that the kingdom of God come quickly. So also the blessed apostle warns, forming and strengthening the firmness of our hope and faith. Nothing, he says, have we brought into this world, and truly we cannot take anything away. Having therefore sustenance and covering, with these we are content. But those who want to become rich fall into temptation and snares and many harmful desires which plunge a man into destruction and ruin. For the root of all evils is greed, which some pursuing have made shipwreck of the faith and have pierced themselves with many sorrows.

choices.why: Keeps the concrete Latin term for worldly display, which Cyprian contrasts with spiritual grace.
Matches the petition for daily bread and the literal sense of diurnum as belonging to a day.

choices.english: to stretch out the desires of his petition into the long term
choices.why: Preserves the spatial metaphor of extending desires over time, which Cyprian uses to contrast with daily asking.
rejected: to prolong the desires of his petition
to extend his petition's desires far

choices.english: sufficient for the day is its own evil
choices.why: Keeps the exact biblical wording Cyprian quotes, including the possessive sua, and the literal sense of malitia as evil or trouble.
rejected: each day has enough trouble of its own
the day's own trouble is enough for it

choices.why: Exhibitio here means provision or support, and tegumentum means covering or clothing; both are concrete terms for basic needs.

choices.english: have made shipwreck of the faith
choices.why: Preserves the vivid metaphor of shipwreck, which Cyprian takes from Paul and which fits the theme of being plunged into ruin.
rejected: have suffered shipwreck in the faith
have been shipwrecked from the faith

pass_b_english: But it can also be understood this way: we who have renounced the world and cast away its riches and pomps through the faith of spiritual grace should ask for ourselves only food and sustenance. The Lord instructs this when he says, "Whoever does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple" (Luke 14:33). And whoever has begun to be Christ's disciple, renouncing everything according to his teacher's voice, ought to ask for daily food and not stretch out the desires of his petition into the long term. The Lord himself again prescribes this, saying, "Do not think about tomorrow, for tomorrow will think about itself. Sufficient for the day is its own evil" (Matthew 6:34). Rightly, then, does Christ's disciple ask for sustenance for the day, since he is forbidden to think about tomorrow. It would be contradictory and self-defeating for us to seek to live long in the world when we pray for the kingdom of God to come quickly. So also the blessed apostle warns, forming and strengthening the firmness of our hope and faith: "We brought nothing into this world, and we cannot take anything out. Having sustenance and covering, with these we are content. But those who want to become rich fall into temptation and snares and many harmful desires, which plunge a person into destruction and ruin. For the root of all evils is greed, and some, reaching for it, have made shipwreck of the faith and entangled themselves in many sorrows" (1 Timothy 6:7-10).

problems.why: 'inseruerunt se' means 'they have inserted/entangled/involved themselves', not 'pierced themselves'. 'Inserere' is to insert, plant, or involve in; the metaphor is of entangling oneself in sorrows, not piercing.
problems.ruling: 'inseruerunt se' = 'inserted/entangled themselves'; 'pierced themselves' is wrong, changing meaning.

fixed: Changed 'pierced themselves' to 'entangled themselves' because 'inseruerunt se' means they inserted or entangled themselves in sorrows, not pierced themselves.

last_rejected.quote: through the faith of spiritual grace
last_rejected.why: Latin 'fide' is ablative of 'fides' (faith), but here means 'by faith' or 'in faith'; 'gratiae spiritalis' is genitive, 'of spiritual grace'. The English makes 'faith' modify 'grace' rather than being the means by which they renounced.
last_rejected.ruling: 'fide gratiae spiritalis' rendered as 'faith of spiritual grace' is within normal range; ambiguity reflects Latin's compressed ablative-genitive construction.

last_rejected.why: 'in diem' means 'for the day' in the sense of 'day by day' or 'daily', matching 'diurnum cibum' earlier. 'Sustenance for the day' is ambiguous; it could mean 'for that particular day' rather than 'as a daily provision'.
last_rejected.ruling: 'uictum sibi in diem' as 'sustenance for the day' is within normal range; 'in diem' can mean daily provision, no meaning lost.
